LS5008/30 –
Revisiting Microorganisms
Dr Lewis C. E. Mason
BSc (Hons), MSc, PhD, FIBMS, MRSB, AFHEA
Module Leader
L.Mason@Kingston.ac.uk

Learning objectives
• Recall structures and their functions within the prokaryotic
bacterial cell
• Explain how structures contribute to bacterial function, 
survival, and adaptation
• Evaluate contemporary research (Mason et al., 2026)
regarding the association between microbial features and 
epidemiological / outbreak ‘success’

functions

But… do all bacterial cells carry 
the same structures?
The bacterial cell wall

Normal bacterial transcription animation
Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oC21vLFtsjo

Normal bacterial translation animation
Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oC21vLFtsjo

animation
Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IkKZ_gxAOXI
1
2
3

Patterns of microbial growth
•
Lag phase:
Little to no change in the number of microbes, but 
metabolic activity is high. Adjusting to the new
environment.
•
Log phase:
Microbes multiply at a constant, rapid rate.
•
Stationary phase:
The growth medium is depleted of nutrients and/or
toxic metabolites accumulate.
•
Death phase:
Microbes die due to the lack of appropriate nutrients
and the buildup of toxic metabolites
Microscopic structures of a bacterium

What is considered a ‘microscopic’ structure?
• ‘Microscopic’ structures are defined as structures that 
cannot be directly visualised with the naked eye, and 
require a microscope (light/electrons) to view
• These can be structures at a cellular or sub-cellular
level (µm–nm) requiring a light-microscope or 
electron microscope, respectively
• There are some nuances with this – for example, the slime
layer is a microscopic structure, but its effects can be 
visually seen by the naked eye on agar (glossy colonies)

Capsule
Acinetobacter calcoaceticus
• Some bacteria are able to produce a bacterial 
capsule (outer protective layer)
• Capsules can have a variety of purposes:
immune evasion; environmental survival;
enhanced attachment; biofilm formation.
• Shigella sonnei, Streptococcus pneumoniae, 
Neisseria meningitidis, Escherichia coli K1 
are some examples of bacteria that benefit 
greatly from their capsule when it is produced
Capsule

Extracellular polymeric substances (EPS)
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
EPS
• The EPS is the entire extracellular matrix
produced by microbes
• It includes polysaccharides, proteins,
DNA, water, lipids, and other trapped
substances
• EPS is essential for Pseudomonas 
aeruginosa to form chronic biofilms

slides.topic: •  Some bacteria have what is known as a ‘slime layer’,
slides.text:
•  Some bacteria have what is known as a ‘slime layer’,
formed from EPS.
•  Different to a capsule, it is not 
organised tightly and it is not easily removed. 
•  Slime layers aid in adhesion, biofilm 
formation, and offer a barrier against 
antibiotics and the immune system.
Slime layer
Staphylococcus epidermidis
Slime layer

Surface layer (‘S-layer’)
• The S-layer is a 2D sheet of protein
that self-assembles into a crystalline 
structure
• It is incredibly highly organised, 
similar to chainmail
• There are a wide variety of S-layer
structure types, which influence their
function (protective exoskeleton,
molecular sieve, adhesion, etc.)

Fimbria (plural: fimbriae)
Fimbria
• Fimbriae are short, thin, (usually) 
numerous non-retractable 
hair-like structures carried by 
some bacteria
• Their main purpose is for
adhesion to surfaces,
particularly host surfaces/tissues
• The fimbriae tips have adhesion
proteins for this purpose
Escherichia coli

Conjugation pilus
•
Bacteria may use a 
conjugation pilus structure to allow
plasmid DNA to be replicated
and transferred directly from one
bacterium to another
•
Conjugation may occur
between different strains,
species, and even genera
of bacteria
Conjugation 
pilus
Escherichia coli

Type IV pilus
Type IV
pilus
•
The Type IV pilus structure allows bacteria
to adhere to surfaces, undertake ‘twitching motility’,
and uptake DNA
•
This pilus type extends and retracts,
which allows the twitching movement
and uptake of DNA
•
Usually long, and fewer quantities
than fimbriae
Neisseria sp.

Type III Secretion System (T3SS)
•
The Type III Secretion System
apparatus is a nano-sized molecular
machine, resembling a syringe, 
produced by some Gram-negative 
bacteria
•
Its purpose is to inject bacterial effector
proteins (usually virulence factors)
into the cytoplasm of host cells, 
modulating the immune system etc.
Shigella sonnei Type III 
Secretion System

Flagellum (plural: flagella)
Flagella
Campylobacter sp.
•
The flagellum is a long structural
appendage carried by some bacteria
for ‘swimming’/swarming motility
•
The flagellum rotates like a propellor,
and is very effective for movement in
a liquid
•
Bacteria can either carry zero, one,
two, or many flagellum/flagella

Endoflagellum (EF) / Axial Filament
Treponema pallidum
• The endoflagellum / axial filament
is used by spirochetes for motility
via corkscrew motions
• This is very effective for movement
through even viscous liquids, and
also to penetrate tissues
• This motility is particularly useful for
bacteria to swim through mucus and semen

Outer membrane vesicles (OMVs)
Salmonella sp.
•
Gram-negative bacteria can produce OMVs, 
which may contain a variety of proteins, 
lipids, enzymes, and even DNA
•
They act as nano-sized delivery parcels,
and can be used to shuttle toxins, adhesins,
among others, to the host cell
•
OMVs can be involved in immune evasion,
defence and stress survival, antibiotic
resistance mechanisms, biofilm formation, etc.

Cytoplasmic inner membrane (‘plasma membrane’)
• The thin lipid bilayer that surrounds the bacterial
cytoplasm
• Has a swathe of functions: cell division & organisation;
biosynthesis; energy release; transport & uptake; selective barrier

Gram-positive cell wall
• The Gram-positive cell wall protects the bacterium
from osmotic lysis, gives it shape and rigidity,
and provides a surface for environmental/host 
interaction
• The thick peptidoglycan
layer allows the structure
to resist internal pressure
• The teichoic acids aid in
adhesion / immune interaction

Gram-negative cell wall
• The peptidoglycan layer in
a Gram-negative cell wall is thinner
• Unique to Gram-negative bacteria,
the outer cell membrane acts as a 
selective barrier
• The lipopolysaccharide (LPS)
layer is hyper-immunogenic, 
eliciting a strong host immune 
response

Mycolic-acid-rich outer layer
sp.
•
Mycobacterium tuberculosis is unique in that its outer layer
is neither Gram-positive or Gram-negative
•
Its mycolic-acid-rich envelope makes it hydrophobic and have a 
reduced permeability, particularly useful for drug tolerance

slides.topic: Bacteria with no cell wall structure (‘mollicutes’)
slides.text:
Bacteria with no cell wall structure (‘mollicutes’)
•
Some bacteria have no cell wall structure at all,
including Mycoplasma spp.
•
Having no cell wall has some benefits:
- Intrinsic resistance to β-lactam antibiotics
- High deformability
- Less immunogenic
- Less fitness cost to the bacteria
Mycoplasma genitalium

Nucleoid
• The nucleoid is a non-membrane-bound
region within the bacterial cytoplasm
• Most of the cell’s DNA is contained
within the nucleotide, within the
circular chromosome of the nucleoid
• Bacterial DNA is highly compact,
via negative supercoiling and looping
in domains
• Some bacteria can have multiple chromosomes

Plasmids
• Plasmids are small circular structures of ‘extra’
DNA carried by some bacteria
• They often carry virulence and/or 
antimicrobial resistance genes
• A plasmid that replicates well in 
one bacterium may not necessarily
replicate well in another. Plasmids
may also have a fitness cost for bacteria.
Plasmids in Escherichia coli

Prophage DNA
Escherichia coli (blue) surrounded by 
T4 bacteriophages (green)
• Bacteriophages (viruses that infect bacteria)
can ‘inject’ their DNA into a bacterium
• This DNA is then structurally incorporated
into plasmids or the core chromosome
of a bacterium
• The DNA injected by the bacteriophages
may also encode ‘useful cargo’ genes, 
such as exotoxins, virulence factors, 
antimicrobial resistance genes, etc.

slides.topic: The shape of a bacteriophage virus is incredible!
slides.text: The shape of a bacteriophage virus is incredible!

70S Ribosomes (50S + 30S)
• Bacteria have a prokaryotic 70S ribosomal structure
(50S + 30S)
• The ribosome is the site of
protein synthesis, converting
messenger RNA (mRNA)
into functional proteins via
translation 
• The protein synthesis process
can have interesting nuances
among bacterial species

Endospores
Clostridium difficile
• Endospores are dormant, metabolically inactive
survival forms developed within a cell when
conditions are poor for survival of a bacterium
• The structure formed allows the spore to
resist disinfectants and other environmental
pressures
• Only a small minority of bacteria are able to
produce endospores: Bacillus spp. and
Clostridium / Clostridioides spp.

Cell shape
• Cell shape is determined by
the peptidoglycan architecture
and various cytoskeletal proteins
• The MreB and FtsZ proteins allow
a bacterial cell to elongate, 
resulting in the bacillus shape
• Different shapes have different
surface areas, motility, 
attachment, immune evasion, etc.
capabilities

Cell arrangement
• Cell arrangement is
determined by 
division plane patterns
and whether daughter 
cells are completely 
separated, attached,
or semi-detached
• When a bacterial cell 
divides, a septum is
formed and the location 
of this influences arrangement

Cell size
Thiomargarita magnifica
Mycoplasma agalactiae
• Bacterial cells can vary significantly
in size
• Many factors influence the size of a 
bacterium… division timing, placement,
structural components, homeostatic
and growth physiologies, cell-cycle
and DNA replication lengths
• Cell size has implications for ecology,
survival, diffusion, and energy
requirements
Macroscopic structures of a bacterium

What is considered a ‘macroscopic’ structure?
• ‘Macroscopic’ structures are defined as structures that 
can be seen with the naked eye, and do not require a 
microscope to view.
• Macroscopic structures are usually formed from large 
populations/communities of bacteria (e.g. a colony), 
not just a single cell.
• Structures that are 0.1–0.2 mm are potentially visible, anything
>1mm is clearly visible. These are all macroscopic.

Colony size
• A colony is a clearly visible mass of bacteria,
grown on a surface such as an agar plate
• While it varies by species, each colony 
has around 105 – 109 bacterial cells within
• A single colony on its own is usually 
assumed to be clonal, meaning all of the 
bacterial cells within a single colony are
usually genetically identical
Escherichia coli

Colony form/shape
• Motility, adhesion, cell separation, growth rate, environment,
quorum sensing, all influence typical colony form structure

Colony margin
• Bacterial colony margin structures may also differ
• This is influenced by motility, adhesion, cell separation,
growth rate, surfaces, environment, quorum sensing,
genetics, among other factors
• Remember, a colony has millions of bacterial cells

Colony elevation
•
The elevational structure of a bacterial colony may
also differ among species of bacteria
•
Elevation is influenced by growth rate, presence of
EPS, capsules, motility, and spreading across the plate

Colony surface texture
•  There are many different colony surface structural textures:
- Smooth / glistening
- Rough / granular / matte
- Rugose / wrinkled
- Mucoid / slimy / gummy / shiny
- Powdery / chalky / velvety / fuzzy
• Differences can be seen between and even within species, 
due to EPS/capsule/motility/growth/environment

Colony opacity
•  Opacity is defined as the ‘measure 
of how much an object or material 
blocks light from passing through it’
•  Bacterial colonies can be 
transparent, translucent, iridescent, 
or opaque
•  The thickness of the colony and cell 
packing, size, shape, capsule, EPS, 
pigments, and other factors 
influence this

Colony consistency
•  Bacterial colonies may have different consistencies
between and within species:
- Creamy/buttery/pasty
- Mucoid/slimy/stringy
- Dry/crumbly/friable
- Chalky/powdery
- Tough/rubbery/leathery
- Viscid (‘ropy’)
• Influenced by water content,
extracellular polymers
(capsules, slime, etc.), and cell-wall physiology
Hypermucoid Klebsiella pneumoniae

Colony pigmentation
•  The pigmentation (‘colour’) of 
bacterial colonies is influenced 
by small molecular structures 
known as pigments
•  Bacterial colonies can appear 
as many different colours: 
white, cream, grey, yellow, 
gold, orange, pink,
red, blue, violet, brown, black
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Serratia marcescens
Chromobacterium violaceum
Staphylococcus aureus

Biofilms
Rogers, Adams, Rode (2011)
Plastic Surgery International Journal
Medical image of a child
with Pseudomonas 
aeruginosa biofilms 
following a facial burn
(the patient then fully 
recovered
after one month)
• Bacterial biofilms are a structured 
community of bacterial cells,
attached to each-other and/or
to a surface via an extracellular
matrix produced by the bacteria
• Biofilms are often mixed species,
though some may be of a single
species
• Biofilm formation involves initial
attachment, EPS production, and quorum communication

Spreading patterns
•  Bacterial colonies of distinct species may 
present a distinct spreading pattern 
structure on different agar plate types, 
associated with surface-motility
• Patterns may include: swimming, 
swarming, chemotactic rings, twitching, 
gliding, and sliding
• These macroscopic-visible structures
are often the result of microscopic
structures of the bacteria (flagella, etc.)

Colony structures on different agars
•  There are many types of agar that can be 
used to grow bacteria. Some agars are 
differential, selective, or even both. 
• Differential agars have properties which 
visualise specific characteristics of bacteria
• Selective agars have specific nutrients to 
encourage growth of specific bacteria, and/or 
substances that inhibit the growth of other 
bacteria
MacConkey Agar

•
Bacterial taxonomic classification is ‘the process of 
organising bacteria into a hierarchical system of 
groups (‘taxa’) based upon their shared genotypic & 
phenotypic characteristics, and evolutionary 
relationships’
•
Bacterial taxonomic classification is a polyphasic-
informed process: phenotype, chemistry, and 
genetics/genomics
What is bacterial taxonomic classification?

•
International Code of Nomenclature of Prokaryotes 
(ICNP)
•
International Committee on Systematics of Prokaryotes 
(ICSP)
•
International Journal of Systematic and Evolutionary 
Microbiology (IJSEM)
•
List of Prokaryotic Names with Standing in 
Nomenclature (LPSN)
Who decides bacterial taxonomic classification?

Example of bacterial taxonomy
Bacteria (Domain)
Eubacteria (Kingdom)
Pseudomonadota (Phylum)
Gammaproteobacteria (Class)
Enterobacterales (Order)
Enterobacteriaceae (Family)
Shigella (Genus)
Shigella sonnei 
(Species)
Constituents of the name of a bacterium
(E.g. Shigella sonnei)

Proper taxonomic nomenclature
•
“Shigella sonnei is my favourite species of bacteria to research”.
•
“Shigella spp. cause shigellosis, an enteric disease”.
•
“The agar plate had colonies of a single Shigella sp. growing on it”.
•
“Shigella sonnei (S. sonnei) is rod shaped. S. sonnei is also 
Gram-negative”.
- Bacterial genus and species names must only be underlined (instead of italicised) in handwritten work. 
The sentences above are only underlined for demonstrative purposes, and you must use italics only
when typing out bacterial names in digital work.
- sp. = singular, one species
- spp. = plural, multiple species 
- The genus starts uppercase (Shigella), the species ‘epithet’ (sonnei) starts lowercase

More resolute classification systems (‘typing schemes’)
Shigella sonnei (species)
3 (lineage)
CC152  (clonal complex)
Shigella flexneri (species)
3a (serotype)
Salmonella enterica (species)
Typhimurium (serovar)
ST19 (sequence 
type)
ST152 
(sequence type)
3.6.1.1.2  
(genotype)
CC1 (clonal complex)
• These further definitions of a species
are based upon biochemical features and 
genetic content of a bacterium, and are useful 
in the outbreak investigation of closely related
bacteria of the same species

Genomics influencing bacterial taxonomic classification
• Genomics is now the backbone of bacterial 
taxonomic classification, but it is not the sole factor 
considered
•
1960 – Taxonomy began to incorporate genotypic features like G+C content and DNA-
DNA hybridization
•
1977 – 16S rRNA phylogeny influences evolutionary relationships at higher-level 
classification
•
1990 – 16s rRNA sequencing influences systematics and influences species boundaries
•
2005, 2006, 2007 – Whole genome sequencing metrics influence species boundaries
•
2015 onwards – Genome-based taxonomy dominates

slides.topic: Biochemical test results influencing bacterial taxonomic
slides.text:
Biochemical test results influencing bacterial taxonomic
classification
• The results of a plethora of biochemical 
tests were the central defining feature of 
genera and species in the past
(pre-1960s)
• Carbon-use, fermentation, indole,
methyl red, Voges-Proskauer, citrate 
utilisation, oxidase, nitrate reduction, 
catalase, urease, coagulase, DNAase, B-
galactosidase, H2S production, hydrolysis, 
salt tolerance, etc.
Biochemical test 
strips

Temperature-requirements influencing bacterial 
taxonomic classification
• Bacteria that are adapted to extreme 
temperatures (psychrophilic and thermophilic) 
may be taxonomically classified due to 
this physiological trait
• The Thermus genus is heavily influenced by 
temperature physiology

Atmospheric-requirements influencing taxonomic 
classification
• The oxygen requirements (aerobic, anaerobic, 
microaerophilic) of a bacterium often have 
deep-rooted physiological impacts
which may inform taxonomic classification
• Campylobacter spp. were separated from 
Vibrio spp. as the former require a 
microaerophilic atmosphere, while the 
latter are facultatively anaerobic
Campylobacter spp.
Vibrio cholerae

Microscopic structures influencing bacterial taxonomic 
classification
• Microscopic structures are still cited in taxonomic 
descriptions, as part of the ‘polyphasic’ consideration
• Cell shape, size
• Cell arrangement
• Cell wall (Gram reaction, etc.)
• Endospores
• Motility
• Capsule 
• Everything else we discussed before…

Macroscopic structures influencing bacterial taxonomic 
classification
• Macroscopic structures are also described in taxonomic
descriptions, and some can be quite indicative of taxonomy
• Colony morphology (margin, elevation, size, form/shape)
• Surface texture and consistency
• Pigmentation
• Spreading patterns
• Biofilm formation
• Everything else we discussed before…

History influencing bacterial taxonomic classification
• Historical factors may influence the initial
taxonomic classification of a bacterium, which 
then may be kept into the future
• Shigella spp. were identified as ‘dysentery 
bacillus’ by Kiyoshi Shiga in 1898
• Genomics has now revealed that Shigella 
lineages are EXTREMELY genetically close to E. coli, 
and some scientists now describe Shigella spp. as 
‘E. coli in disguise with a large invasion plasmid’
Dr Kiyoshi Shiga

Clinical symptoms influencing taxonomic classification 
• The Shigella genus has been kept distinct 
from Escherichia coli partly due to its 
relatively distinct clinical symptoms too
• Shigella causes shigellosis: invasive 
dysentery (bloody diarrhoea, often 
mucus-filled). A painful feeling of needing to 
go to the toilet, even when the bowels are 
empty, is indicative of shigellosis too
• Though, the symptoms are similar to 
Enteroinvasive Escherichia coli (EIEC)…
Shigella sp.

Ecological niche influencing bacterial taxonomic 
classification
• Ecological niche (a bacterium’s specific 
role/location in its ecosystem) can have an 
influence on bacterial taxonomic 
classification
• The Prochlorococcus genus has ecotypes
influenced by presence in high-light
and low-light conditions
Prochlorococcus sp.

The slide 29 reference to nucleotide has been treated as a typo for nucleoid.
